blocks.content: In the earlier Classes and Objects topics, you saw private fields like balance protected from outside code. But how does the language actually enforce that protection, and why are there four different levels of it instead of just one "hidden" switch?
Access modifiers are the keywords, public, protected, package-private (the default, no keyword at all), and private, that control exactly who is allowed to see or touch a field, method, or class.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

An access modifier is a keyword placed before a field, method, or class that controls which other pieces of code are allowed to access it. Java gives you four levels, from most open to most restrictive: public, protected, package-private (no keyword), and private.

Without access modifiers, every field and method in every class would be reachable from anywhere. A BankAccount’s balance field could be directly overwritten by completely unrelated code with no validation at all, no insufficient-funds check, no audit trail, nothing. Access modifiers are what make encapsulation (introduced in the Classes topic) actually enforceable by the compiler, rather than just a polite suggestion.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847709135-520216383.png
blocks.alt: A house showing four zones of privacy from the open front yard to a locked private diary

blocks.content: Think of your own house. The front yard is visible to literally anyone walking by, that is public. The shared hallway inside an apartment building is open to everyone living in that building, but not to strangers off the street, that is package-private. The family room is open to your immediate family and close relatives even if they live elsewhere, that is protected. And your locked personal diary is for you and only you, that is private.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847707197-176566819.png
blocks.alt: The four access levels narrowing from public down to private

blocks.content: Each level is strictly narrower than the one before it. Public is the widest circle, private is the smallest, and every level in between trades off some visibility for some protection.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition

Access modifiers solve the problem of uncontrolled access to a class’s internals. Every class has some details that are safe to expose (a public deposit method) and some that are dangerous to expose directly (the raw balance field). Without a language-enforced boundary, there would be nothing stopping any code, anywhere in a large codebase, from reaching in and corrupting an object’s internal state.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: An access modifier is a keyword (public, protected, or private, or the absence of one for package-private) applied to a class, field, method, or constructor that defines the scope from which it can be legally referenced, enforced by the compiler at compile time and re-checked by the JVM at class-loading time.
4. Key Terminology

["public: accessible from any class, in any package.","protected: accessible within the same package, plus any subclass in a different package.","package-private (default): accessible only within the same package, no keyword needed, this is what you get if you write no modifier at all.","private: accessible only within the exact same class that declares it.","Encapsulation: the broader design goal (from the Classes topic) that access modifiers are the enforcement mechanism for.","API surface: the subset of a class (usually its public members) that other code is meant to depend on.","Information hiding: deliberately keeping implementation details inaccessible so they can change later without breaking other code."]
items: public: accessible from any class, in any package.
protected: accessible within the same package, plus any subclass in a different package.
package-private (default): accessible only within the same package, no keyword needed, this is what you get if you write no modifier at all.
private: accessible only within the exact same class that declares it.
Encapsulation: the broader design goal (from the Classes topic) that access modifiers are the enforcement mechanism for.
API surface: the subset of a class (usually its public members) that other code is meant to depend on.
Information hiding: deliberately keeping implementation details inaccessible so they can change later without breaking other code.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847711163-319209453.png
blocks.alt: A BankAccount class with one field and methods spread across three different access levels

blocks.content: Notice that a single class routinely mixes access levels: balance stays private so nothing outside the class can corrupt it directly, deposit and withdraw are public because that is the intended way for other code to interact with the account, and getBalanceForAudit is protected so only trusted subclasses can peek at the raw value.
6. Syntax & Code Example
The modifier keyword always comes first, right before the field or method type. Leaving the keyword out entirely gives you package-private, there is no explicit keyword for that one:

codes.python:
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__balance = 100  # only this class can touch it directly (name-mangled)

    def deposit(self, amount):  # any code can call this
        self.__balance += amount

    def some_helper(self):  # public by default in Python
        return self.__balance / 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    wallet = Wallet()
    wallet.deposit(50)
    print(wallet.some_helper())

blocks.content: ["private fields are the safest default for any piece of state a class needs to protect.","public methods form the class’s real \"contract\" with the rest of the program.","protected sits between package-private and public, specifically to support inheritance across packages."]

public methods form the class’s real "contract" with the rest of the program.
protected sits between package-private and public, specifically to support inheritance across packages.

public void deposit(...) / withdraw(...) are the intended entry points, Main can call these freely because they are public.
protected double getBalanceForAudit() is invisible to Main (a completely unrelated class), but visible to SavingsAccount specifically because SavingsAccount extends BankAccount.
applyInterest() inside SavingsAccount calls getBalanceForAudit(), this compiles only because of the protected relationship granted by inheritance.

All of this only works because the compiler is silently checking every single access along the way:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847714520-623344353.png
blocks.alt: The compiler checking every access modifier before allowing code to compile

blocks.content: If you uncommented account.balance in Main, the compiler would reject the program before it ever runs, private access violations are caught at compile time, not at runtime like a null check would be.
9. Behind the Scenes (Compiler and Bytecode Verification)
blocks.text: 9. Behind the Scenes (Compiler and Bytecode Verification)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847715982-145898473.png
blocks.alt: Access checked twice: once by javac, once again by the JVM bytecode verifier

blocks.content: Access control is not just a courtesy performed by the compiler. When javac compiles your source, it checks every field and method access against its declared modifier and refuses to compile violations.
9.1 A Second Check at Class-Loading Time
blocks.text: 9.1 A Second Check at Class-Loading Time

blocks.content: Separately, when the JVM loads compiled .class files, its bytecode verifier independently re-checks access rules again, this exists specifically to guard against someone hand-crafting or tampering with .class files to bypass the compiler’s checks. Access control is enforced at two separate layers, not just one.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847717673-57939733.png
blocks.alt: Access modifiers protecting sensitive internals across e-commerce, banking, social and gaming domains

blocks.content: ["E-commerce: internal pricing/discount calculation logic stays private, only a public getFinalPrice() method is exposed.","Banking: the raw balance field stays private, exactly like the BankAccount example above.","Social Media: a stored password hash stays private, only public methods like verifyPassword() are exposed, the hash itself is never directly reachable.","Gaming: a character’s health field stays private, changed only through a public takeDamage() method that can enforce rules like a minimum of zero."]
items: E-commerce: internal pricing/discount calculation logic stays private, only a public getFinalPrice() method is exposed.
Banking: the raw balance field stays private, exactly like the BankAccount example above.
Social Media: a stored password hash stays private, only public methods like verifyPassword() are exposed, the hash itself is never directly reachable.
Gaming: a character’s health field stays private, changed only through a public takeDamage() method that can enforce rules like a minimum of zero.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847719308-850479000.png
blocks.alt: A private field exposed only through a stable public getter/setter API

blocks.content: Nearly every class in the Java standard library follows this exact convention: private fields, public getters and setters. This is precisely what lets libraries change their internal field layout across versions without breaking code that depends on them, the public API stays stable even when private internals change.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Enforces encapsulation at the language level, not just by convention.","Overusing public can quietly turn a class’s entire internal state into a permanent, hard-to-change contract."],["Lets a class change its private internals freely without breaking other code.","protected is easy to misuse, since it leaks state to any future subclass, even ones you cannot predict today."],["Catches accidental misuse at compile time instead of at runtime.","Package-private can be too restrictive across large codebases split into many packages by feature rather than by trust boundary."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Making every field public \"to save time,\" which quietly deletes all the protection encapsulation was supposed to provide.","Using protected as a default \"just in case a subclass needs it,\" when package-private or private would have been safer.","Forgetting that package-private has nothing to do with folder structure, it is tied to the declared Java package name, not the file’s location on disk.","Assuming protected members are hidden from unrelated classes in the same package, they are not, package-private access already covers that."]
items: Making every field public "to save time," which quietly deletes all the protection encapsulation was supposed to provide.
Using protected as a default "just in case a subclass needs it," when package-private or private would have been safer.
Forgetting that package-private has nothing to do with folder structure, it is tied to the declared Java package name, not the file’s location on disk.
Assuming protected members are hidden from unrelated classes in the same package, they are not, package-private access already covers that.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Start every field as private by default, and only widen access when there is a concrete, justified reason to.","Expose behavior through public methods (like deposit()) rather than raw public fields, so validation rules stay enforceable.","Reserve protected specifically for members genuinely meant to support future subclassing, not as a lazy middle ground.","Keep a class’s public surface small and intentional, it is effectively a promise to every piece of code that depends on it."]
items: Start every field as private by default, and only widen access when there is a concrete, justified reason to.
Expose behavior through public methods (like deposit()) rather than raw public fields, so validation rules stay enforceable.
Reserve protected specifically for members genuinely meant to support future subclassing, not as a lazy middle ground.
Keep a class’s public surface small and intentional, it is effectively a promise to every piece of code that depends on it.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["Access modifiers control who can see or touch a field, method, or class: public, protected, package-private, or private, from widest to narrowest.","private is the safest default, it protects a class’s internals so only the class itself can touch them directly.","protected specifically supports inheritance across packages, package-private supports trust within one package.","Access is enforced twice: once by the compiler at compile time, and again by the JVM’s bytecode verifier at class-loading time.","A small, intentional public API surface is what lets a class’s internals evolve safely over time."]
items: Access modifiers control who can see or touch a field, method, or class: public, protected, package-private, or private, from widest to narrowest.
private is the safest default, it protects a class’s internals so only the class itself can touch them directly.
protected specifically supports inheritance across packages, package-private supports trust within one package.
Access is enforced twice: once by the compiler at compile time, and again by the JVM’s bytecode verifier at class-loading time.
A small, intentional public API surface is what lets a class’s internals evolve safely over time.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "what is the difference between protected and package-private," the fastest correct answer is: package-private is visible only within the same package, protected extends that same-package visibility to also include subclasses declared in other packages.
